text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: NORA
text: It's ten thirty at night. Someone is scrolling on their phone, sees an advert for a free first laser hair removal treatment, and thinks, why not. They tap through, they've got a question about whether it works on their skin type, and they want to book for Saturday.

speaker: JAMES
text: And in a traditional clinic, that moment is lost. The front desk closed at seven. By the time someone calls back the next afternoon, the person has forgotten, or booked with a competitor, or just changed their mind.

speaker: NORA
text: So the whole business can depend on what happens in the next five minutes after someone taps an advert.

speaker: JAMES
text: For a company that grows through introductory offers and paid advertising, I'd say that's almost literally true. And that's why today's company is interesting. A major software vendor in its industry has named it as one of the most advanced users of AI agents built to answer calls, follow up on leads and keep clients coming back.

speaker: NORA
text: Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. This series follows the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills. Today it's SEV, sometimes written Sev Laser, and lately branded SEV Skin, a chain of medical spas built around laser hair removal.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we begin. Everything we discuss comes from public sources as of November 2026: the private equity firm's announcement, trade and local press, software vendor releases and the company's own website. When something is our opinion or an inference, we'll say so. When a number comes from the company or a vendor, we'll flag it. And because we'll be talking about cosmetic medical treatments, nothing here is medical advice, and nothing is investment advice either.

speaker: JAMES
text: And a caveat specific to today. The public record on SEV is patchy and sometimes contradictory. Different sources give different headquarters, different store counts, and, notably, different chief executives. We'll walk through those conflicts honestly rather than pretend we know which is right.

speaker: NORA
text: So give me the one-line version.

speaker: JAMES
text: SEV is a multi-state medical spa chain, founded in Southern California in 2010, that offers laser hair removal as its core service, plus injectables, microneedling, facials and body contouring, at published, relatively accessible prices, with free introductory treatments and low-cost memberships. It has grown from twenty-seven offices in 2023 to more than fifty, by its own count.

speaker: NORA
text: And the AI angle?

speaker: JAMES
text: In April 2026, the medspa software company Zenoti announced an expanded set of AI agents it calls the AI Workforce, and named SEV as among the most advanced operators on it. That's a vendor claim, and we'll unpack exactly what it does and doesn't tell us.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's start with basics. Where is SEV, and how big?

speaker: JAMES
text: Headquarters is where it gets slightly messy. The private equity firm's page and its 2023 announcement say Burbank, California. A business database and a 2024 local news article give an address in Glendale, California, which is right next door. So, somewhere in the Burbank and Glendale area of Los Angeles. For listeners that distinction doesn't matter much, but it's one of several signs that SEV's public footprint isn't tightly managed.

speaker: NORA
text: And locations?

speaker: JAMES
text: Here's the trajectory, from different sources. Twenty-seven offices in seven states in June 2023, according to the private equity firm's announcement. Thirty by September 2023, according to a profile by the software company Boulevard. More than thirty-five by July 2024, according to a local news article in San Antonio. And over fifty, according to an article in Beauty Independent that isn't dated but looks like it's from 2025.

speaker: NORA
text: So it roughly doubled in two years.

speaker: JAMES
text: If those figures are right, yes. That's fast growth for a clinical business. And the same Beauty Independent piece said SEV had added eight markets in the past year, including Orlando, Phoenix and Boston.

speaker: NORA
text: Where are the clinics concentrated?

speaker: JAMES
text: California and Texas are the heart of it. In May 2025 SEV opened in Sugar Land, Texas, near Houston, and the local news story listed six other Texas locations: Austin, Fort Worth, Frisco, Houston, San Antonio and Dallas. It opened its first Idaho spa, in Meridian, in January 2024. Microneedling is offered in California, New York, Virginia, Texas and Massachusetts, which gives you a sense of the wider footprint.

speaker: NORA
text: People and revenue?

speaker: JAMES
text: Revenue isn't public. A jobs site estimates fifty-one to two hundred employees, but that's an aggregator's estimate, and with more than fifty locations I'd treat it cautiously. Client numbers aren't public either, though SEV told Beauty Independent its client base grew forty-two percent year over year. That's a company figure.

speaker: NORA
text: And who runs it?

speaker: JAMES
text: This is the biggest conflict in our sources. The founder is Sevana Petrosian, and the 2023 private equity announcement and the Beauty Independent article both describe her as chief executive. But the Zenoti press release from the twenty-eighth of April 2026 names Carrie Julier as SEV Laser's chief executive and quotes her. We found nothing else confirming that.

speaker: NORA
text: So either there's been a leadership change, or the vendor got it wrong.

speaker: JAMES
text: Those are the two possibilities, and we don't know which. A succession from founder to a professional chief executive a few years into a private equity hold would be very normal. But we couldn't confirm it, so we'll describe Carrie Julier as the person Zenoti named. And one more name: a January 2024 article said Dr. Ehsan Ali oversees operations.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do the history.

speaker: JAMES
text: SEV was founded in 2010 by Sevana Petrosian. The first location was in Glendale, California, and it was originally called Glendale Laser Center. That's from Boulevard's 2023 profile. So it started as a single local laser clinic, and the name SEV, which obviously echoes the founder's first name, came later as it grew into a brand.

speaker: NORA
text: And it stayed founder-owned for a long time.

speaker: JAMES
text: About thirteen years. Then on the twenty-first of June 2023, Levine Leichtman announced an investment in SEV "in partnership with founder and management". Terms weren't disclosed. It was described as the tenth platform investment of the firm's sixth fund, and the founder stayed on as chief executive at the time.

speaker: NORA
text: "In partnership with founder" is a specific phrase.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is. In private equity, it usually signals that the founder kept a meaningful stake and a leadership role, rather than selling out entirely. That's common in consumer businesses where the founder is closely tied to the brand and the culture. It's also a reason why a later chief executive change, if that's what happened, would be a significant moment.

speaker: NORA
text: What's happened since 2023?

speaker: JAMES
text: Mostly new clinics, as far as we can see. We found no add-on acquisitions under the current owner. The growth appears to be what the industry calls de novo, meaning opening new locations from scratch rather than buying existing spas. Meridian in Idaho in January 2024, San Antonio in July 2024, Sugar Land in May 2025, and the expansion into Orlando, Phoenix and Boston. Plus the service expansion, notably a microneedling device called SkinPen, which SEV describes as cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration, rolling out to more locations in 2026.

speaker: NORA
text: Why de novo rather than acquisitions? A lot of medspa roll-ups buy.

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't know SEV's reasoning. But there's a plausible logic, in our view. If your model depends on a consistent brand, consistent pricing and a consistent digital funnel, it can be easier to open a clean new clinic than to convert someone else's, with its own staff, systems and loyal clients expecting different prices. Acquisitions are faster for footprint, but integration in clinical businesses is notoriously messy.

speaker: NORA
text: So, about three and a half years into this owner's hold.

speaker: JAMES
text: About three years and five months as we record. That's mid-hold. Long enough to have built the growth story, not yet at the point where an exit is the main topic.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about the customer. Who comes to SEV, and for what?

speaker: JAMES
text: The core service is laser hair removal. I'll give a general, non-medical explanation, and listeners should talk to a qualified professional about their own situation. Laser hair removal uses light energy that's absorbed by pigment in the hair follicle. The heat damages the follicle and reduces its ability to grow hair. Because hair grows in cycles and only some follicles are in the right phase at any one time, people typically need a course of several sessions, spaced weeks apart, to see the full effect.

speaker: NORA
text: So it's not a one-off purchase.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly, and that's fundamental to the business. A laser hair removal client is, by the nature of the treatment, a repeat visitor over many months. And after the course, some people come back for maintenance. That repeat pattern is why memberships and packages make sense.

speaker: NORA
text: You mentioned skin type in the cold open. Why does that matter?

speaker: JAMES
text: Again, general background, not advice. Because traditional laser hair removal relies on the laser targeting pigment in the hair rather than the surrounding skin, it has historically worked best where there's strong contrast, dark hair on lighter skin. For people with darker skin, the skin itself absorbs more of the light, which raises the risk of burns or pigment changes if the wrong device or settings are used. Different laser types and settings exist for different skin types, which is exactly why a proper assessment by a trained provider matters.

speaker: NORA
text: So the question Alyssa will ask in our walk-through later is a real one.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's one of the most common questions in the category, in our understanding, and one of the most important to answer carefully. A chain that serves diverse cities like Houston, Dallas and Los Angeles has to be good at this, both clinically and in how it communicates.

speaker: NORA
text: And who's the typical customer?

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't have SEV's demographic data. General knowledge says laser hair removal appeals to a broad range of adults, women and men, who are tired of shaving or waxing. SEV's pitch, as the Beauty Independent headline put it, is an "accessible pricing approach". So the target seems to be the mass market rather than the luxury end. Though it's interesting that a San Antonio local article described SEV as offering "luxury medical spa services". The positioning, in our view, is something like affordable luxury.

speaker: NORA
text: What else do they offer?

speaker: JAMES
text: Beyond laser hair removal, SEV lists injectables, which typically means neuromodulators that relax wrinkles and dermal fillers, plus microneedling, facials and body contouring. Industry research from Grand View says facial treatments are the largest segment of the medical spa market, at about fifty-four percent, and body shaping and contouring is the fastest-growing service.

speaker: NORA
text: So the strategy is to bring people in with laser hair removal and then offer them other things.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's our reading. Laser hair removal is a great entry service. It's a clear need, it's easy to explain, and it requires repeat visits. Each visit is a chance to build trust and introduce something else. Microneedling and injectables tend to be higher-value and also repeat. If a client who came for hair removal later becomes an injectables client, their lifetime value can rise substantially.

speaker: NORA
text: What's the customer's biggest worry?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd guess three. Does it work for me, especially with my skin and hair type. Is it safe, and who's actually doing it. And how much will it really cost, after the free first session. A good clinic answers all three clearly. A great one answers them at ten thirty at night when the customer is asking.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk economics. How does SEV make money?

speaker: JAMES
text: The visible model has four parts. Published prices, free introductory treatments, memberships, and loyalty and referral programs. Let's take them in turn.

speaker: NORA
text: Published prices first.

speaker: JAMES
text: SEV publishes prices by location on its website, which is less common than you might think in aesthetics, where many clinics only quote after a consultation. At the time of our research, for example, full-body laser hair removal was listed at six hundred and fifty-nine dollars in San Francisco and six hundred and nine dollars in Frisco, Texas. Prices may have changed since, and we don't know exactly what's included at each price. But it shows SEV prices by market, presumably reflecting local rents, wages and competition.

speaker: NORA
text: Then the free first treatment.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. A free intro treatment is the hook. It lowers the risk for a nervous first-time customer. The cost to SEV is real, staff time, device time and supplies, so the economics depend on how many of those people convert to paying clients. SEV told Beauty Independent that intro-offer bookings ran at four times the average daily rate per location, which I read as meaning intro offers drive a big volume of bookings, although the exact meaning of that statistic isn't fully clear to us.

speaker: NORA
text: And memberships.

speaker: JAMES
text: SEV advertises memberships starting at fifteen dollars a month. We don't know the details of what each tier includes. But in general, memberships in aesthetics give clients discounts or credits in exchange for a recurring fee. For the business, they create predictable revenue and keep clients coming back. For the client, they make regular treatments feel more affordable.

speaker: NORA
text: And loyalty?

speaker: JAMES
text: There's an app, the SEV Skin app, plus referral programs and a rewards scheme that the website calls the "Sev suite". All of that is designed to keep clients in SEV's own channel, booking directly, rather than through third parties.

speaker: NORA
text: You mentioned advertising. How important is it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Very, in our view. SEV told Beauty Independent that its cost per acquisition, what it spends in marketing to win each new client, fell by eighty-seven percent. That's a company figure, and an eighty-seven percent drop is so large that I'd want to know the baseline and the time period. But it tells you that acquisition cost is a number SEV watches closely. A business that grows through paid advertising and free intro offers lives or dies on how efficiently it turns ad clicks into paying, returning clients.

speaker: NORA
text: So the funnel is: ad, intro offer, booking, first visit, conversion to package or membership, retention, cross-sell.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's it exactly. And every step of that funnel has a leak. People who click and don't book. People who book and don't show. People who come for the free session and never return. Members who lapse. That's where AI comes in.

speaker: NORA
text: How big is the medical spa market?

speaker: JAMES
text: There are numbers, but they disagree, so I'll give them with caveats. Grand View Research estimates the global medical spa market at about twenty-four billion dollars in 2025, rising to about twenty-eight billion in 2026, and projects around seventy-eight billion by 2033, which would be growth of nearly sixteen percent a year. But the same page gives slightly different figures in its summary, so treat it as approximate. Grand View also says North America has about forty-one percent of the global market.

speaker: NORA
text: And the US specifically?

speaker: JAMES
text: Beauty Independent cited a figure of six point nine billion dollars for the US medical spa market in 2024, growing at nearly fourteen percent a year, but didn't name its source. And a 2026 industry piece put broader US aesthetic medicine at anything from about twenty-five billion to about fifty billion dollars, depending on how you define it. The honest summary is: large, growing at double digits by most estimates, and badly measured.

speaker: NORA
text: And laser hair removal specifically?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find a reliable figure. One more structural point from Grand View, though: single-owner providers hold the largest share of the market, about thirty-seven percent. In plain English, this is a fragmented industry dominated by independent clinics. That's exactly the kind of market private equity likes to consolidate.

speaker: NORA
text: So who are SEV's competitors?

speaker: JAMES
text: The closest like-for-like is Ideal Image, a well-known national laser hair removal and aesthetics chain. It's been private-equity backed for years. Search results point to an investment by TPG Growth in May 2021, and Bloomberg reported in 2021 that it was preparing for a possible stock market listing. We couldn't verify current ownership. Then there's Laser MD Medspa, which has grown partly through acquisitions, for example buying Young Medical Spa to expand into Pennsylvania. And Valure Spa and Laser, which a business database lists as a comparable.

speaker: NORA
text: Any others?

speaker: JAMES
text: The same database names a few others, Depil Tech, Shobha, Hair and Skin, and Oliva, but we didn't verify their models or how directly they compete. And, of course, thousands of independent medspas and dermatology practices. There's also more private equity activity in the space, for example a firm called Lead Capital building a day spa platform. Our read is that SEV is competing not just for clients but for the best locations and, in future, for acquisition targets.

speaker: NORA
text: Why is private equity so interested in medspas?

speaker: JAMES
text: A few reasons, in our view, drawn from how the industry generally works rather than anything SEV has said. The market is growing by most estimates. Demand is repeat by nature, which gives predictable revenue. It's mostly cash-pay, so there's less dependence on insurers. And it's fragmented, so a well-run chain with good systems can open or buy clinics and, in theory, run them better than a single owner can, with shared marketing, purchasing and software.

speaker: NORA
text: What's the catch?

speaker: JAMES
text: The catch is that the thing that makes a clinic good is people, and people don't scale as neatly as software. Skilled providers are in demand, clinical standards have to be consistent across many sites, and the brand is only as strong as its weakest clinic. Roll-ups that grow too fast without the operating discipline can end up with uneven quality. And as more investors pile in, prices for good clinics and good locations go up.

speaker: NORA
text: And the software companies?

speaker: JAMES
text: They're not competitors for clients, but they matter enormously. Zenoti and Boulevard are two of the main software platforms for medspas, handling scheduling, payments, charting and client management. Both are now selling AI. Zenoti has its AI Workforce. Boulevard lists an AI receptionist on its site. SEV has relationships with both, at least historically, since Boulevard profiled SEV in 2023, and Zenoti named it in 2026.

speaker: NORA
text: So the AI is coming from the software vendors, not from the clinics.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's one of the big trends in this industry. Medspa chains, even large ones, generally don't build AI in-house. They buy it as part of their operating software. Which raises an interesting question for SEV: if the AI comes from the vendor, and the vendor sells it to everyone, what's SEV's advantage?

speaker: NORA
text: Let's get to that. What exactly did Zenoti announce?

speaker: JAMES
text: On the twenty-eighth of April 2026, Zenoti announced an expansion of what it calls its AI Workforce, which it describes as purpose-built AI agents for every medspa workflow. The agents include an AI receptionist that answers calls, a lead manager that scores and follows up on leads, a retention agent that flags clients at risk of lapsing, and an AI scribe that helps with clinical notes. The release also mentions inventory forecasting.

speaker: NORA
text: Take me through those agents one at a time. What does each actually do, in general?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general terms, based on how these products are described rather than SEV's configuration. The AI receptionist answers phone calls with a natural-sounding voice, handles common questions like opening hours, prices and preparation instructions, and books, moves or cancels appointments directly in the scheduling system. The lead manager takes new enquiries from ads, web forms and calls, scores how likely each is to book, and follows up by text or email, so no lead sits untouched overnight.

speaker: NORA
text: And the others?

speaker: JAMES
text: The retention agent looks across the client base for signs someone is drifting away and prompts outreach. The AI scribe drafts clinical notes from the provider's input. And inventory forecasting predicts what supplies each location will need, which matters when you're using consumables and injectable products that cost real money and have shelf lives. The idea of an "AI workforce" is that each agent covers one job that used to fall between the cracks of a busy front desk.

speaker: NORA
text: And SEV's role in it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Zenoti named SEV Laser as among the most advanced operators on the AI Workforce, and included a quote from Carrie Julier as SEV's chief executive. That's the evidence. It's a vendor's press release, so naturally it presents its customer in the best light. And it doesn't tell us exactly which agents SEV uses, in how many clinics, or with what results.

speaker: NORA
text: What did SEV itself say?

speaker: JAMES
text: Nothing we found, beyond that quote. SEV's own website, as of our research, describes online booking, the app and memberships, but doesn't mention AI features or a chatbot. We found no AI or data roles in its job listings, though the listings we saw didn't show titles. So SEV's public AI footprint is essentially one vendor announcement.

speaker: NORA
text: How much weight should we give it?

speaker: JAMES
text: More than nothing, less than a company disclosure. When a vendor names a customer and quotes its chief executive, the customer has almost certainly agreed to it, so it's a real relationship. "Among the most advanced operators" suggests SEV is using several agents in live operations. My best guess is that at least the AI receptionist and lead follow-up are in use, because those fit SEV's growth model so well. But I want to be clear that's a guess.

speaker: NORA
text: Is buying AI from a vendor a weakness?

speaker: JAMES
text: Not in itself. For a chain of fifty or so clinics, buying is almost certainly the right call. Building your own AI receptionist would be expensive and slow, and the vendor can spread its development cost across thousands of spas. The question is how well you use it. Two chains with the same software can get very different results depending on their processes, data quality, staff training and how they configure the agents.

speaker: NORA
text: So SEV's advantage, if it has one, is in execution.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's our view. Being early on the vendor's most advanced tools gives SEV a learning lead. If it uses that lead to tune its funnel, how it answers questions, when it follows up, what offers it makes to lapsing clients, that's a real edge. But it's an edge that competitors can narrow by buying the same software, so it has to keep moving.

speaker: NORA
text: I want to talk about the people and the clinical side, because this isn't a nail salon. These are medical procedures.
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: JAMES
text: Right, and it's the most sensitive part of the business. In medspas generally, procedures are often performed by trained estheticians, nurses or nurse practitioners rather than by physicians. The rules on who can do what vary by state and by procedure, and I'm not going to try to summarise them. SEV's website mentions things like medical clearance calls, nurse practitioners and devices cleared by the Food and Drug Administration, which indicates the clinical framework it operates in.
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: NORA
text: Is there controversy about that?
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: JAMES
text: There's ongoing debate. A 2024 article we saw cited guidance from the American Academy of Dermatology favouring dermatologist oversight of these kinds of procedures. Dermatologists have an obvious interest in that position, but they also see the complications when things go wrong. Our view is that regulatory scrutiny of the medspa industry is more likely to increase than decrease as it grows.
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: NORA
text: How does AI fit into that?
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: JAMES
text: Carefully, is the answer. There's a clear line between administrative AI and clinical AI. An AI receptionist that books appointments and answers questions about opening hours is administrative. An AI that tells someone a treatment is safe for their skin type is drifting into clinical advice. A responsible medspa needs guardrails. The AI should be able to explain general information and then route medical questions to a qualified person, for example through a medical clearance call.
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: NORA
text: And the AI scribe?
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: JAMES
text: That's an interesting one. An AI scribe listens to or reads a clinician's interactions and drafts notes. That saves time and can improve the quality of records. But clinical records are sensitive health information, so privacy rules apply, and the clinician has to check what the AI wrote. We don't know whether SEV uses the scribe agent.
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: NORA
text: And the front desk staff? How do they feel about an AI receptionist?
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: JAMES
text: It depends on how it's framed, like every story in this series. If the AI answers the calls nobody could answer anyway, at night, during the lunch rush, when the front desk is with a client, then it's filling a gap, not taking a job. The staff can spend more time with the people physically in the clinic. If it's framed as replacing the front desk, morale suffers, and the clinic loses the human warmth that makes nervous first-time clients feel comfortable.
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: NORA
text: You said nervous. This is a personal service.
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: JAMES
text: Very personal. People are talking about their bodies, their skin, sometimes their insecurities. Trust is everything. In our view, AI should make the human part of the experience better, not replace it. Quick answers before the visit, easy booking, sensible reminders. Then a real person who is kind and competent in the treatment room.
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: NORA
text: And data?
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: JAMES
text: A medspa holds health-related information, photos, payment details and treatment histories. AI vendors process some of that. We found no public statement from SEV on AI governance or security certifications. Given the sensitivity, a clear, public privacy and AI policy would, in our view, be a trust builder.
chapter: The clinic floor: people, oversight and trust

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make it concrete. Walk me through a new client, before and with AI. Invented person.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Let's call her Alyssa. She's twenty-nine, lives in a suburb of Dallas, and has been thinking about laser hair removal for a while. One evening she sees an SEV advert on social media offering a free first treatment.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Old way first.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: She taps the ad and lands on the website. She has a question: she has darker skin and has read that some lasers aren't suitable. She can't find a clear answer, so she fills out a contact form. It's nine forty-five at night. The form goes into a queue. The next day, the front desk at her nearest clinic is busy with clients all morning. Someone calls her back at two in the afternoon. She's at work and doesn't pick up. They leave a voicemail. She means to call back, but doesn't. A week later she sees an ad for a competitor and books there instead.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And SEV paid for that click.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. The marketing money was spent, and the lead leaked. Multiply that by every clinic and every evening, and you can see why lead follow-up matters so much.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Now with AI.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Alyssa taps the ad, and either a chat assistant on the website or, if she calls, an AI receptionist responds immediately. She asks about her skin type. The assistant gives her general information, for example that suitability depends on the person and the device, and that a clinician will assess her before any treatment. It offers to book her a free intro session plus a clearance call with a clinician. She picks Saturday at eleven. She gets a confirmation and a reminder the day before.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: So the AI doesn't answer the medical question itself.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: It shouldn't, beyond general information. It routes the question to a person and gets her booked. That's the right design, in our view. The AI's job is speed and convenience. The clinician's job is safety and judgment.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Then the visit.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: She comes in on Saturday, has the intro treatment, and the provider talks her through a recommended course and the membership options. Maybe she doesn't sign up on the spot. In the old world, she might drift away. With a lead manager agent, she gets a well-timed follow-up a few days later, perhaps with a reminder of what was discussed and an easy way to book her next session. If she does sign up, the retention agent starts watching for warning signs.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: What are the warning signs?
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, things like missing an appointment, booking intervals getting longer, not opening messages, or approaching the end of a package. A retention model scores the risk that a client will lapse, and triggers an action, like a friendly check-in or a rebooking prompt, before they actually leave.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Let me do a second one. A clinic manager.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. Let's call him Tomas. He manages an SEV clinic in Phoenix, one of the newer markets. His problems are different from Alyssa's. He has to fill the treatment rooms, especially on weekday mornings, which are quieter. He has to make sure he has the right staff for the booked appointments. And he has to hit targets for new clients, conversions and memberships.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: What does AI do for Tomas?
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Potentially three things. It answers the calls his front desk misses, so fewer leads leak. It gives him a daily list of members at risk of lapsing, with suggested actions, so his team spends their time on the right follow-ups. And, if pricing and capacity tools are used, it could suggest targeted offers to fill quiet slots, for example a reminder to members who prefer mornings. That last one is our suggestion, not something SEV has announced.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And where does Tomas still matter?
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Everywhere that involves people. Hiring and training his providers, keeping the clinic clean and safe, handling the client who had a bad reaction and is upset, building a team that clients like. AI can make his week more efficient, but it can't make his clinic a place people trust.
chapter: A first visit, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Let's be specific about challenges.

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd name five. First, dependence on paid acquisition. SEV grows by winning new clients through ads and free offers. If advertising costs rise, or if social media platforms change their rules for medical and cosmetic advertising, the whole funnel gets more expensive. The reported eighty-seven percent drop in acquisition cost shows how much effort goes into this, and how sensitive the business is to it.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, price competition. Published prices and free intro offers are now common across the industry. Ideal Image, Laser MD and countless independents compete for the same clients in the same cities. If everyone is offering a free first session, it stops being a differentiator and becomes a cost of doing business. Margins could get squeezed.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, clinical and regulatory risk. As medspas grow, scrutiny of who performs procedures, how they're supervised and how they're advertised is likely to increase. Any incident, at any clinic, can damage the brand. And with more than fifty locations across many states, keeping clinical standards consistent is a big operational job.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, inconsistency in the public record, which I'd treat as a symptom rather than a problem in itself. Different headquarters, different store counts, a chief executive named by a vendor but not confirmed elsewhere. For clients that doesn't matter. But for future buyers, partners and regulators, a clear, consistent public story helps. Our view is that SEV would benefit from a stronger corporate communications presence.

speaker: NORA
text: And fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fifth, the vendor-led AI question we've already raised. If SEV's AI is Zenoti's AI, then any competitor on Zenoti can get similar tools. SEV's advantage has to come from how well it uses them, which means investing in the people, processes and data around the software, not just paying the licence.

speaker: NORA
text: You haven't mentioned the economy.

speaker: JAMES
text: It belongs on the list. Cosmetic treatments are discretionary. In a downturn, people may delay or cancel. Memberships help, because they create a habit and a commitment, but they also lapse when budgets tighten. We have no specific data on how SEV's business moves with the economy.

speaker: NORA
text: Okay, opportunities. Where would you push?

speaker: JAMES
text: The first is the obvious one: an AI front desk and booking conversion layer across every clinic. Answer every call and web chat, at any hour, book the intro session, confirm and remind, and follow up with people who don't book. The value levers are front desk labour hours and recovered revenue from leads that would otherwise leak. We can't size it without SEV's call and lead volumes, which aren't public.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, membership retention. Score every member for lapse risk and trigger the right action at the right time. Even a small improvement in retention on a large membership base adds up, because retained revenue has no acquisition cost. And that directly offsets the dependence on paid ads.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, cross-selling microneedling and injectables into the laser base. With SkinPen rolling out to more locations in 2026, SEV has an existing base of laser clients who already trust it. AI could identify which clients are most likely to be interested, based on age, treatment history and expressed interests, and time the suggestion well. That has to be done tastefully. Nobody wants to be told their skin needs work.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, location-level pricing and capacity. SEV already prices by market. With good demand data, it could set price bands and offers to fill quiet times and protect busy ones. Airlines and hotels have done this for decades. In a clinic it has to be gentler, because clients notice if prices jump around, but targeted offers for off-peak times are a sensible start.

speaker: NORA
text: Fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fifth, growth itself. More clinics in existing clusters, like Texas, where SEV already has density and brand awareness. And possibly add-on acquisitions of independent medspas in those clusters, following the firm's multi-unit playbook. No add-on deals have been announced, so that's speculative. And replicating the Texas formula in newer markets like Phoenix, Orlando, Boston and Idaho.

speaker: NORA
text: Anything on the clinical side?

speaker: JAMES
text: The AI scribe, carefully used, could reduce documentation time for providers and improve record quality, which also helps with compliance. And AI could help with consistency across clinics, for example by flagging unusual patterns in treatment notes or outcomes for a clinical leader to review. Those are our suggestions, and they'd need strong governance.

speaker: NORA
text: If you had to pick one AI bet for the next eighteen months?

speaker: JAMES
text: The AI receptionist and booking conversion layer for inbound calls and web leads across all locations, with membership retention scoring on top. SEV's growth runs through paid intro offers and bookings, so every lost call and every slow follow-up costs money directly. The value levers are front desk labour and revenue from intro-offer leads. And the tools are already available from a vendor SEV works with, so it's about execution rather than invention.

speaker: NORA
text: First hundred days?

speaker: JAMES
text: Days one to thirty: measure the leak. Pull data on inbound calls, missed calls, web leads, time to first response, booking rate, show rate and conversion from intro to paid, by clinic. Most chains are surprised by how many calls go unanswered. Confirm exactly which AI agents are live, where, and how they're configured. Appoint one owner with authority across marketing, operations and clinical.

speaker: NORA
text: Days thirty to sixty?

speaker: JAMES
text: Pick a group of clinics, say ten, with a mix of mature and new markets. Make sure the AI receptionist and lead follow-up are fully switched on and properly configured there, with clear clinical guardrails: general information only, medical questions routed to a person. Compare their funnel numbers with similar clinics that haven't changed. At the same time, build or switch on retention scoring and give clinic managers a short daily list of at-risk members.

speaker: NORA
text: And sixty to a hundred?

speaker: JAMES
text: Measure and decide. Did response time drop? Did booking and show rates rise? Did intro-to-paid conversion improve? Did member lapses fall? Listen to clients and staff, too. Were any clients frustrated by the AI? Did the front desk find it helpful? Then roll out across the network with the configuration that worked best, and set targets.

speaker: NORA
text: And the metric?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cost per retained client. Not cost per click, not cost per booking. The total marketing and service cost to get someone who's still a client six months later. That's the number that tells you whether the funnel is healthy, and AI should push it down.

speaker: NORA
text: Second-best bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cross-sell intelligence for the SkinPen and injectables rollout. It builds on the same client data and turns the laser base into a platform for higher-value services.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's step back. What can other businesses learn from SEV?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd pull out four. First, for many businesses, the best AI is bought, not built. SEV didn't need an AI lab. It needed a software vendor with good agents, and the willingness to be an early, serious user. If you're a multi-site service business, look at what your operating software vendor already offers before building anything.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, buying the AI isn't the advantage, using it is. Two clinics with the same software can get very different results. The advantage comes from configuration, process, staff training and measurement. Treat a vendor AI rollout as an operating change, not an IT project.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, find the leak in your funnel. Every business that pays to acquire customers has places where those customers fall out: unanswered calls, slow follow-ups, no-shows, lapses. AI is very good at plugging exactly those leaks, because they're about speed and persistence, which software does well and busy humans do badly.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, draw the line between administrative and expert AI. In any business that involves professional judgment, medical, legal, financial, let AI handle speed and convenience, and route anything requiring judgment to a qualified person. That protects customers and protects the business.

speaker: NORA
text: And a fifth, about the public story?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. Tell your own story. Right now, the most visible description of SEV's AI comes from a vendor's press release, and the public record has inconsistencies on basic facts. A company that clearly explains its own approach, including how it uses AI responsibly, builds trust with clients, staff and future investors.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's run the risks.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, AI disintermediation of booking. If consumers start booking through general-purpose AI assistants or aggregator platforms, SEV's direct channel and app could weaken, and acquisition costs could rise. That's speculative but worth watching. Two, price pressure from Ideal Image, Laser MD and the independents. Three, dependence on paid acquisition. Four, regulatory action on clinical staffing or advertising. Five, discretionary demand in a downturn.

speaker: NORA
text: Explain the disintermediation risk a bit more. How would that actually happen?

speaker: JAMES
text: Picture a year or two from now. Instead of searching and tapping an ad, a consumer asks the AI assistant on their phone to find a well-reviewed laser hair removal clinic near them with a Saturday slot under a certain price, and book it. That assistant compares options and books wherever it can. If SEV's booking system is easy for those agents to use, SEV could win. If it isn't, SEV is invisible. And if an aggregator sits in the middle, it may charge a fee for every booking.

speaker: NORA
text: So the clinic stops owning the first conversation.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the worry. Today SEV pays advertising platforms for attention. Tomorrow it might pay AI platforms for bookings. Our view is that the defence is the same as always: strong reviews, a brand people ask for by name, and a membership base that books directly because it's easier. It's speculative, but it's the kind of shift a growth model built on paid acquisition should be thinking about now.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the owners?

speaker: JAMES
text: Mid-hold, the job is to prove the model scales profitably: more clinics, healthy unit economics and strong retention. A buyer will look hard at clinical governance and at whether the growth depends on ever-rising marketing spend. A well-documented AI funnel that lowers cost per retained client would be a strong part of the story.

speaker: NORA
text: What should listeners watch?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four things. First, confirmation of SEV's leadership. Is Carrie Julier the chief executive, and what's the founder's role? Second, any SEV-authored statement about its AI, with specifics on which agents are live and what they've achieved. Third, the SkinPen and injectables rollout in 2026, as a sign of the cross-sell strategy. And fourth, whether SEV starts acquiring independent medspas or stays with new openings.

speaker: NORA
text: And what's not public that you'd want?

speaker: JAMES
text: Revenue, clinic-level economics, membership numbers and retention rates, call answer rates, and any clinical incident data. Those would tell you whether the growth is sustainable and how much AI is really contributing.

speaker: NORA
text: Quick-fire round. Short answers.

speaker: JAMES
text: Go.

speaker: NORA
text: Laser clinic or medspa?

speaker: JAMES
text: A medspa that uses laser hair removal as its front door.

speaker: NORA
text: Most valuable asset?

speaker: JAMES
text: A growing base of repeat clients who already trust it with their skin.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest weakness?

speaker: JAMES
text: Dependence on paid acquisition, and a patchy public story.

speaker: NORA
text: Most important AI tool?

speaker: JAMES
text: The AI receptionist. The cheapest client to win is the one who already tapped your ad.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest AI bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: Booking conversion plus membership retention, across every clinic.

speaker: NORA
text: Should AI give medical advice in a medspa?

speaker: JAMES
text: No. General information and booking, yes. Judgment stays with qualified people.

speaker: NORA
text: One thing every multi-site service business should do this quarter?

speaker: JAMES
text: Count your missed calls. Then decide whether you can afford them.

speaker: NORA
text: Optimist or pessimist?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cautious optimist. The model is clear and the tools exist. The risks are clinical and competitive, not technological.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me try a summary. SEV was founded in 2010 by Sevana Petrosian as Glendale Laser Center, and grew into a medspa chain with more than fifty locations by its own count, concentrated in California and Texas, after Levine Leichtman invested in partnership with the founder in June 2023. Its model is accessible, published pricing, free intro treatments, low-cost memberships and a digital funnel, with laser hair removal as the entry point and microneedling and injectables as the next step. Its AI story so far is a vendor's: Zenoti named SEV among the most advanced users of its AI agents in April 2026, quoting Carrie Julier as chief executive, which we couldn't confirm elsewhere. The opportunity is to plug every leak in the funnel, from unanswered calls to lapsing members, while keeping clinical judgment firmly with people. The risks are acquisition costs, price competition and regulation.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's it. And the lesson for other businesses is that buying AI is easy. Being the customer who gets the most out of it is the hard part, and the advantage.

speaker: NORA
text: Next time on Portfolio Deep Dives, episode thirty, our final episode of the series, we finish on something sweet, with Kilwins, the chocolate, fudge and ice cream franchise headquartered in Petoskey, in northern Michigan.
